abstract: Imaging-based spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at single-cell resolution, but imperfect segmentation often misassigns transcripts between neighboring cells, a problem known as transcript spillover. This spillover is niche-dependent and can therefore confound downstream analyses that rely on niche-specific differential expression. True spillover cannot be directly quantified in experimental ST data, so existing correction methods infer contamination indirectly from transcript positions or expression structure. Here we introduce SYNDRI, a post-segmentation correction method that frames spillover detection as a supervised, gene-level classification task. We develop SYNDRI-SIM to generate labeled training data by simulating spillover between spatially mapped scRNA-seq profiles. SYNDRI uses a transformer to predict gene-level spillover probabilities conditioned on each cell's expression, identity, and local neighborhood, without requiring transcript-level coordinates or deconvolution. On held-out simulated data, SYNDRI achieves an AUPRC of 0.86, compared with 0.64 for the next-best method. Across MERFISH, CosMx, and Xenium datasets, SYNDRI achieves the highest aggregate performance across metrics of cell-type separation, reference similarity, and preservation of within-cell-type heterogeneity. In a CosMx lung cancer dataset, SYNDRI removes nearly all potentially contaminating tumor and macrophage markers from differential expression between tumor-associated and stromal fibroblasts while retaining native fibroblast markers. These results demonstrate the utility of learning from simulated spillover to improve the interpretation of spatial gene expression.
